title: RNNs, attention & Transformers
blurb: Recurrent summary, its issues, attention, masked self-attention

hook.title: One sticky note vs the whole notebook
hook.text: To predict the next word of “My friend opened the …” an **RNN** reads one word at a time and keeps a **single sticky note** $h_t$ summarising everything so far, overwriting it each step. It works for any length, but the note must squeeze in the entire history and you can't read ahead in parallel. **Attention** gives you the whole notebook plus an index: ask a question (the query), score every earlier page (key), and read mostly the relevant ones.
hook.recall: Remember the sticky note vs the notebook: RNNs compress history into one hidden vector processed sequentially; attention looks back at everything in proportion to relevance and, with masking, stays autoregressive.

explore.intro: Tokens: “My friend opened the door”. Keys are fixed directions; you control the query.
tasks: Aim the query at “friend”. How are the weights distributed?
Switch to the self-attention matrix. Turn the mask on and off.
explore.takeaway: Query · keys → softmax → weighted sum. Masked self-attention lets position $i$ see only $\le i$, keeping the autoregressive factorisation while allowing parallel computation.

build.prompt: Order the steps of an attention mechanism (slide 21).
items: Compare the current hidden state (query) to all past hidden states (keys), e.g. by dot product
Build an attention distribution over the history with a softmax
Construct a summary of the history as a weighted sum
Use the summary and current hidden state to predict the next token
build.explanation: Exactly the four bullets of the attention slide.

questions.prompt: How does the number of parameters of an RNN depend on the sequence length $n$?
options: It is constant w.r.t. $n$ ($b_0, W_{hh}, W_{xh}, W_{hy}$)
questions.explanation: The same weights are reused at every step: one sticky-note routine for any length.

questions.prompt: Which statement about RNNs is FALSE?
options: They can be applied to sequences of arbitrary length
Likelihood evaluation is sequential, which makes training slow
Exploding/vanishing gradients occur when accessing information from many steps back
Generation can be parallelised across time steps
questions.explanation: Generation is sequential in *any* autoregressive model: you need token $t$ before sampling $t+1$.

questions.prompt: Attention scores for three past tokens are $(\ln3,\,0,\,0)$. What is the attention weight on the first token after softmax?
Why do generative Transformers use **masked** self-attention?
options: To preserve the autoregressive structure (a token can’t attend to future tokens)
questions.explanation: Black tape again: the future must be hidden to keep $p(x_t|x_{<t})$ valid.

questions.prompt: In attention, what is compared to the *keys* to build the attention distribution?
questions.explanation: Query vs keys by dot product, then softmax.

questions.prompt: *“Transformers beat RNNs because they can generate all tokens in parallel at test time.”* What’s the error?
options: Autoregressive generation is still sequential; the Transformer’s advantage is parallel *training/likelihood evaluation* (no recursion)
Transformers cannot be parallelised at all
questions.explanation: Sticky-note vs notebook changes how history is read and trained, not the fact that you must write the next word before the one after.
